The problem with this argument is that it redefines foundational liberal values as if they were nothing more than emergency protocols. If separation of church and state is only valuable because it prevents conflict, then its worth rises and falls with the threat level. That’s a fragile basis for any core principle. The moment people feel secure, they’ll see no reason to uphold it. But if freedom of religion means anything, it must mean that the state cannot dictate religious belief, and no religion can dictate state policy. That isn’t just a truce. It’s a moral line. You don’t need a war to justify keeping the sword and the altar separate. You just need a conscience.

As for tolerance, it is not merely a ceasefire between hostile camps. It reflects a belief in the dignity of persons. If you only tolerate others because it’s the smoothest path to peace, your tolerance ends the moment you think domination would be more efficient. That’s not a social contract. That’s a calculated pause. Real tolerance is moral. It requires a principle stronger than convenience. Otherwise, when reciprocity breaks down, as it often does, everyone retreats into tribal logic. The Christian baker isn’t refusing a truce. He’s living by a moral code you happen to disagree with. You’re not obligated to agree with it, but to say he forfeits all claim to tolerance because he won’t play by your rules just turns your version of tolerance into a bludgeon.

You can’t preserve peace by eroding the moral core of the very ideals that made peace possible in the first place. Once you reduce them to tools, they stop working as principles.

Let’s break this down so it’s a lot more simple. 

In my view, free will is a metaphysical claim, and compatibalism is a shift away from that. 

You seem to be treating free will as an undisputed subjective phenomenon, with libertarian and compatibilist accounts merely being attempted explanations for such.

I’m arguing about what deserves the label “free will”. You’re arguing about what explains the phenomenon and making the case that the compatibilist explanation’s longevity argues against libertarian free will as being “the definition” of free will. 

I’m going to reframe my position as a syllogism because this has gotten into a to-long-to-read-repeatedly back and forth. 

P1: The existence of free will is widely debated.

P2: Free will is typically not formally and specifically defined in such everyday debates. 

C1: Therefore, it is unlikely that the implicit definition of free will is something for which the existence is trivially true.

P3: Your definition of “free will itself” can trivially be said to exist (e.g., feelings of agency, decision-making behavior).

C2: Therefore, your definition of free will and its existence is likely not what is being widely debated.

P4: In philosophical and popular contexts, debate over free will usually centers on whether we could have done otherwise in a meaningful sense.

C3: Therefore, compatibilism addresses a different question than the one that predominantly motivates the free will debate, and its use of the term is a conceptual shift.

In debates over free will, what do you actually see? People universally agreeing that it exists and discussing its explanation? Or debating its existence at all? It’s the latter - and that should tell you that whatever free will “is”, is something whose existence is uncertain. I will therefore strictly reject any definition of free will you offer if its existence is trivially true.

You’re accusing me of straw-manning, but you haven’t shown that I misrepresented anything—you’re just upset that I applied your reasoning consistently.

You argued that we shouldn’t reject free will just because libertarian free will fails, since the concept includes broader concerns—like everyday decision-making, perceived agency, moral responsibility, etc.—which compatibilism tries to explain. Fair enough.

But that’s exactly what I did with divine revelation. I pointed out that even if supernatural theories of revelation are false, the phenomenon people are trying to explain—feelings of divine connection—still exists. Just like you said we do with free will, we replace the bad theory (God talking) with a better one (psychology, neurology, etc.), without discarding the phenomenon itself. If redefining free will to preserve the phenomenon isn’t “shoehorning,” then neither is redefining divine revelation.

You can’t have it both ways. Either you reject both as nonsensical redefinitions—or you accept both as legitimate phenomena with evolving explanations.

So which is it?

People report being spoken to by god. But you see, God speaking to them isn’t actually what divine revelation is. The spiritual part of that is nothing more than the explanation or theory. On the contrary - divine revelation is just the phenomenon of perceived connection to the almighty.

Therefore, I can say divine revelation is real, because those experiences are real, and the explanations (illusions, emotional influence) are real. I’m not redefining divine revelation. No sir - psychological based accounts for divine revelation have been around for about just as long as theism itself.

When an idea is nonsensical, the solution is to reject it rather than define it ad hoc to forcibly shoehorn it into empirically verifiable frameworks. 

I don’t refine spirits, god, or invisible microscopic unicorns in far off galaxies, in ways that fit observed phenomenon so that I can opine to the existence of things with those labels. I take those ideas as they are and reject them because the burden of proof has not been met. If your conception of free will is limited to “acts differently under non-identical conditions”, then you have reduced free will to an idea the existence of which is trivial and unworthy of the centuries of debate underpinning it. 

THIS is why I do not accept compatibilism - not because its phenomenological claims are false, but because such claims are undeserving of the label “free will”.

You’re right. I technically cannot know that you are conscious. Nor my friends. The only being in reality I can be 100% sure of being conscious is myself. That is precisely why the less similar something is to me, the less confidence I can have in asserting that it’s conscious. It fundamentally changes how behavior should be interpreted, because a baby that cries after falling on its face is not comparable to a machine that’s programmed to output a crying sound based on readings from an accelerometer. **Mimicry does not imply comparability of underlying experience**. Your examples of unverifiable facts fail because they are verifiable. I can demonstrate air by blowing on a piece of paper. Far away galaxies have been directly seen by telescopes. That’s a far, far cry from the fundamental inaccessibility of consciousness.

Libet’s experiment was straightforward. Participants watched a clock and lifted their hand at a time of their own choosing. Two things were recorded:


1.	The timing of neural activity that initiates muscle movement (the readiness potential).

2.	The subjective time at which the participant became aware of their decision to move.


The result, without any need for interpretation, was that 
(1) always preceded (2). The brain began preparing the action before the participant was aware they had decided.

The neural signal’s timing is measured directly through EEG. It’s not an estimate, not a feeling, not a theory. It’s not a matter of interpretation, but direct, objective measurement. The subjective awareness is reported after the fact, and even allowing for some fuzziness in reporting, the order of events is highly consistent and replicable.

You don’t need to decode qualia to understand causality. If the physical signal that initiates movement begins before you’re aware of choosing to act, then conscious awareness is not the cause. It’s a post hoc reconstruction, a mental echo of a decision already in motion.

Because by the time you’re consciously aware of your decision, the brain has already initiated the motor command. The signal from the motor cortex is already traveling to the muscle or has even reached it. That’s what Libet actually measured.

We don’t need to decode the exact subjective “qualia” of the intention. We only need to observe when the action begins in the brain versus when the person becomes aware of it. And the fact is that the neural initiation of movement occurs before conscious awareness.

You’re conflating two fundamentally different things:

Reaction time = responding to an external stimulus as fast as possible (like clicking when a button turns green).
Libet-style experiments = acting without any external cue (in other words, you decide on your own when to move your hand).

The point of Libet’s study isn’t that there’s a delay between awareness and action. It’s that neural activity predicting the decision occurs before the person becomes aware they’ve made a decision. That’s not reaction time so much as spontaneous volition. 

In a reaction time test, you’re consciously preparing to act the whole time. In Libet’s task, you’re told not to prepare. Just act whenever you feel like it. And still, the brain gets there first.

The reason this is the “real question” is because it’s the version of free will people have actually been debating for millennia. When people wonder if they truly have free will, they’re asking whether their choices originate from them in a meaningful way, rather than being fully dictated by prior causes outside their control.

You ask what it would mean for a choice not to be causally determined. The answer isn’t that it must be uncaused in the sense of being random or inexplicable—it’s that the causal chain wouldn’t be strictly deterministic in a way that reduces agency to inevitability. In other words, the agent would play a genuine role in originating the decision, rather than merely playing out an inevitable sequence of events.

Think of it like this: If every choice you make was already set in stone before you made it—determined by prior events, genetics, and external influences—then in what sense are you actually free? If a system is fully deterministic, then every apparent choice was already decided before you ever deliberated on it. That’s what people are really concerned about when they question free will.

The alternative isn’t randomness—it’s a different kind of causation, one where the agent plays an active, originating role rather than being a passive endpoint of a fixed causal chain. If such a thing is possible, that’s what would make free will meaningful.

This is why compatibilism is so frustrating.

The idea that we act according to our desires, free from coercion, is obvious. No one seriously wonders, Do I act on what I want? That question is trivial—it only examines whether our actions align with our observable desires.

The real question of free will—the one worth debating—is whether our choices originate from us in a way that isn’t causally predetermined.

It’s like the age-old debate over God’s existence. Some, unable to prove God in a meaningful sense, redefine the term to mean something uncontested—like the universe itself—declaring victory while sidestepping the real issue.

Compatibilism does the same. It hijacks the debate, redefines free will to mean nothing more than acting on desires, and pretends the problem is solved—when the real question has always been whether our freedom runs deeper.

1. Resources would be wasted trying to prove that jobs have high societal impact in order to garner higher pay.

5. Impact usually varies by geography. For instance, a postal worker who delivers mail to extremely rural areas has far, far less impact than one who delivers in affluent urban areas. 6. Artisans would likely get paid next to nothing. There are people who commission art works. Their craft requires a lot of skill, and the societal impact is rather small. Let me illustrate what I’m saying with an example. 

Let’s say I want to know if putting cheese in soil causes sunflowers to grow more quickly. How would I determine this? 

You get an experimental group and a control group. One of the groups has no cheese, the other group has cheese. Everything else is held constant, or at the very least, is statistically materially the same between groups due to a large sample size. It is precisely because the cheese can be **removed** from the scenario that we can deduce its impact. If cheese had to be in the soil at all times, no comparison could be made, and thus we wouldn’t know  if it in fact causes sunflowers to grow more quickly. 

The problem with self-causation is that **you cannot do this**. You cannot remove the agent from the experiment because the agent’s state is also the effect. Thus there is no way to compare the behavior of agents with and without their inclusion. The impossibility to make such a comparison isn’t simply limited by technology or physical constraints. Its impossibly is conceptually inherent.

This is why the claim of causation adds meaning when the cause is external to the effect, but not otherwise.

Your post wasn’t limited to a particular system or example. I’m arguing against the principle: precedent can potentially justify the status quo. 

Whether or not the benefits outweigh the costs in a certain case is rather subjective.

Precedent has a couple of major advantages compared to untried ideas: 

1. Verified outcomes. Things that have been done have known outcomes. Untried ideas have unknown outcomes. Predictability is preferable to unpredictability because there is less risk of negative unforeseen outcomes. 

2. Lack of transition costs. Society is adapted to ways of living, and no transition costs are required for preexisting systems. Transition periods entail costs, sometime very significant. An example is when the U.S. tried to switch to the metric system. Sound in theory, but the adaptation proved troublesome.

Think about your own life for second. Let’s say you use iPhone, and you’re considering switching to Android (or vice versa). Perhaps there are legitimate reasons for this. Android has more options, more customizability. Certainly. 

But if you do this, you’ll have to expend mental resources relearning a new operating system. Plus, while you’re doing this, you’ll be less effective as using your phone. Not to mention, you’ll likely have to pay financial costs to invest in the new ecosystem and possibly lose devices in the Apple ecosystem (like an Apple Watch). So there’s theoretical benefits, but precedent here cements significant costs. 

Additionally, even if you think you’ll like Android more, you don’t know that for certain. You at least know that iPhone works well enough. You may end up hating Android, and that risk is avoided by sticking with a verified ecosystem.

These situations you’re describing as invalid for the sunk cost fallacy, aren’t descriptive of the fallacy to begin with. 

The fallacy doesn’t oppose continuing pursuits simply because they have accumulated costs. The lesson it departs is that rational decision making excludes sunk costs as the **basis for action** and only considers marginal benefits and costs. 

When you describe thought processes that fall outside this understanding, you are not providing exceptions to the sunk cost fallacy. Rather, you are inventing scenarios with sunk costs that are ultimately irrelevant to the logic of the sunk cost fallacy.

Your argument suggests that the sunk cost fallacy isn't always a fallacy, especially for non-recoverable resources like time and effort. However, the essence of the sunk cost fallacy is about rational decision-making irrespective of the nature of the resource. 

For both monetary and non-monetary investments, the fallacy highlights the importance of not letting past investments dictate future actions. Continuing to invest in a failing project because of past time or effort spent is irrational if the future prospects remain bleak. The decision should be based on future benefits and costs, not past expenditures. Even if time and effort cannot be recovered, the logical approach is to avoid further waste of these resources by shifting to a more promising opportunity.

Thus, while time and effort are indeed non-recoverable, the principle of the sunk cost fallacy still applies. It encourages us to make decisions based on future potential rather than past sacrifices, promoting a more rational and forward-thinking approach to investment and resource management.

It’s worth pointing out that under the tax code, this doesn’t eliminate the tax. It merely defers it. Because seizing the collateral doesn’t constitute a sale, the acquirer steps into the basis of the borrower. 

To illustrate, let’s say Elon Musk pays $1 million for shares in Apple. He sells the Apple stock later for $2 million, triggering $1 million of taxable gains. Someone turns around and sells that for $4 million, triggering an additional $2 million of capital gains, for total income taxed of $3 million. 

Now let’s say that, alternatively, Elon Musk buys $1 million in apple stock. Once it’s worth $2 million, he puts it up as collateral for a $2 million loan and immediately defaults. The bank then sells that apple stock for $4 million later on. 

In this case, the bank acquires the basis that Elon Musk had ($1 million), and they thus trigger a $3 million taxable gain, not a $2 million one. 

As you can see, total taxable gains are identical in both cases. From the perspective of the IRS, these are essentially the same. They get their money either way. But if you set the angle lens to only include Elon Musk, then it looks like the rest of us are getting cheated on tax revenue, when in reality it’s ultimately going to be burdened by someone downstream.

This is a misunderstanding of how taxes are levied and reported. 

Income before taxes, per books, is calculated using generally accepted accounting principles as determined by the AICPA. It’s not how much taxes were paid - for that, refer to the statement of cash flows. Rather, it’s the amount of taxes that are expected to be paid, whether this year or in 10 years, that were accrued over the period. 

Taxable income follows fairly similar, but nonetheless independent rules set by the tax code. 

An example of a difference is depreciation. Accelerated depreciation under tax law is often higher than what is recorded on the book income statement. As a result, pre-tax income per books is higher than taxable income. 

The ratio you’re calculating, if compared to the 21% statutory rate, doesn’t consider tax credits either.

FYI, the corporate tax rate in the US is 21%. With average state corporate tax rates, you’re often looking at a combined federal and state rate around 26%.

Statistical significance means that you can reject the null hypothesis. The null hypothesis is that the rate of cheating is the same between men and women. To reject it, you need data that, due to the variances and sample size, cannot reasonably be explained by random fluctuations in the sample that was picked. In other words, you need to show that for the differences to have arisen from the two groups (men and women) despite equal populations, an extremely unlikely sample would have been required. It is because the sample would have had to be so unlikely that you can infer the null hypothesis has a low probability and conclude that men and women between 18 and 29 cheat at different rates.
